Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The work is framed around solving clinical/therapeutic biofeedback training problems (helping children with FASD/ADHD self-regulate) and focuses on designing a general biofeedback mechanism (overlays, multimodal cues) to work with existing entertainment games. The primary design driver is the utilitarian biofeedback mechanic and clinical training goals, with fun leveraged via off-the-shelf games rather than co-designed or repurposed primarily for fun, matching a mostly utility-first design.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The system is a biofeedback overlay applied to arbitrary off-the-shelf games (e.g., Portal, Nail'd). The paper does not constrain or modify the underlying game turn structure; it only obscures visuals continuously based on physiological state. Given no explicit turn/phase mechanics and that the example games are real-time action titles typically played with simultaneous continuous actions, the best-fit category is entirely simultaneous.

        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),

reasoning: The system overlays biofeedback-driven visual obfuscation in real time on top of existing off-the-shelf games, and the textures are rendered and varied continuously based on the user’s current physiological state. This implies a real-time, synchronous interaction loop tightly coupled to ongoing gameplay, with no mention of turn-based or delayed/asynchronous mechanics introduced by the study design.

        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The system modifies single-player off-the-shelf games by overlaying visual obfuscation based solely on the player’s own physiological state; there is no indication of multiple roles, players, or asymmetric information/abilities. The underlying games (e.g., Portal, Nail’d) are standard single-player experiences, and the biofeedback overlay applies uniformly to that single player, making the effective game structure symmetrical in the sense of the rubric.
